config.title: Quantifying Pedagogical Camouflage in Higher Education
config.author: Danielle N. Gray-Singh, Ph.D.

statements.statement: True learning requires grappling with unscripted ambiguity that cannot be captured by a standardized rubric.
I deliberately design assignments where initial student failure is an essential step toward conceptual breakthrough.
Creative insight in my discipline emerges from non-linear, messy synthesis that resists algorithmic evaluation.
I intentionally rephrase experimental teaching ideas into corporate jargon (e.g., 'applied learning') to pass curriculum review.
I describe open-ended classroom exploration as 'measurable skill acquisition' on official course documents to avoid scrutiny.
I align my assignment rubrics with institutional assessment metrics even when I know they flatten critical student thinking.
I encourage students to challenge core disciplinary assumptions, even if it derails the planned lesson schedule.
I use institutional buzzwords in my syllabi primarily to signal compliance to department chairs and deans.
Generative AI tools are best used to streamline student output to meet standardized workplace deliverables.
Over-reliance on AI drafting tools risks smoothing away the idiosyncratic, divergent friction essential to human thought.
I structure my syllabus around deep conceptual questions rather than granular, auditable learning outcomes.
I enforce strict adherence to rubric criteria to protect my course evaluations from student appeals.
In laboratory or seminar sessions, I prioritize productive tangents over rigid coverage of content modules.
I frame creative cross-disciplinary assignments under safe, established labels like 'interdisciplinary synthesis.'
Standardized rubrics provide the only objective and equitable basis for evaluating student work across diverse cohorts.
Evaluating student creativity requires holistic, subjective judgment that cannot be reduced to a numerical point grid.
I regularly modify course plans mid-semester in response to unanticipated student curiosity and creative detours.
I censor or downplay high-risk pedagogical experiments unless they are backed by published 'evidence-based' literature.
Deep pattern recognition in my field requires an imaginative leap that goes beyond systematic data correlation.
Curricular standardization ensures institutional quality control and protects program accreditation metrics.
I utilize automated LMS grading tools to manage heavy teaching loads, even if it limits qualitative feedback.
Rewarding student intellectual risk-taking requires accepting unconventional project formats that violate standard rubrics.
I explicitly inform students that unscripted discovery is more valuable than arriving at a predetermined 'correct' answer.
I feel pressure to present my teaching as a series of predictable, scalable steps rather than an organic, evolving process.
The most profound moments in my teaching occur when both I and my students do not know the exact outcome of an exercise.
I adopt administrative jargon in grant proposals to maximize funding potential, regardless of actual project execution.
Detailed learning outcomes and transparent rubrics are essential tools for promoting student equity and clarity.
Standardized metrics penalize necessary scientific or artistic failure, forcing students into risk-averse compliance.
I reserve space in my course design for spontaneous student-led inquiry that is completely detached from formal assessment.
I frame collaborative student play as 'team-based problem solving' to align with institutional career-readiness initiatives.
AI prompt engineering represents a vital new form of structured, efficient academic literacy.
True critical thinking is inherently non-algorithmic and cannot be replicated by probabilistic language models.
I view pedagogical friction and confusion as productive cognitive states rather than instructional failures.
I align my course learning objectives directly with university-wide strategic planning goals.
I limit open-ended classroom debate to ensure all mandated curriculum content is covered before final exams.
I prioritize process portfolios (showing drafts and pivots) over polished, convergent final products when assigning grades.
